title: Insert Interval
statement: You are given a list of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start time, and one new interval. Insert the new interval so that the list stays sorted and non-overlapping, merging with any intervals it overlaps. Return the resulting list. You may not modify the input in place.
realWorld: Adding a booking to a calendar that is already tidy. The stored blocks are sorted and disjoint by construction, so re-sorting everything to add one meeting is wasted work — the insert should cost a single pass, and on a calendar with thousands of blocks, a binary search for the landing spot makes it cheaper still.

examples.explanation: [2,5] overlaps [1,3] (2 <= 3), so they merge into [1,5]. [6,9] starts after 5 and is untouched.
[4,8] overlaps [3,5], [6,7] and [8,10]. Their union is [3,10]; [1,2] and [12,16] are untouched.
The new interval is fully contained. The merged end must remain 5, which is what Math.max guarantees.

constraints: intervals is sorted by start_i ascending and its members do not overlap each other

bruteForce.idea: Append the new interval to the list, sort everything by start, and run the standard merge sweep.
code: public static int[][] insert(int[][] intervals, int[] newInterval) {
Arrays.sort(all, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));   // re-sorting an already-sorted list
if (open == null || current[0] > open[1]) merged.add(new int[]{ current[0], current[1] });
bruteForce.whySlow: It is correct, and in an interview it is a fine first answer to state before improving. But it throws away the one thing the problem hands you for free: the list is already sorted and already disjoint. Sorting n+1 elements to place one of them is paying O(n log n) for information you were given.

patternIdentification: Sorted and disjoint input means the intervals fall into exactly three consecutive runs relative to the new one: those that end before it starts, those that overlap it, and those that start after it ends. Because the list is sorted, those runs are contiguous — so one left-to-right pass with three phases does the job, and no comparison is ever needed between two existing intervals.

optimized.idea: Walk the list once in three phases. Copy every interval ending strictly before the new one starts. Then absorb every interval that overlaps, widening the new interval with `min` of the starts and `max` of the ends, and append it once the run is over. Finally copy the rest unchanged.
code: public static int[][] insert(int[][] intervals, int[] newInterval) {
// 1. Everything that finishes before the new interval begins is unaffected.
// 2. Everything starting at or before the (growing) end overlaps — absorb it.
end = Math.max(end, intervals[i][1]);   // max: a contained interval must not shrink it
// 3. The tail starts after the merged block ends; nothing left to do.

complexity.time: O(n) — each interval is visited by exactly one of the three phases
complexity.space: O(n) for the output; O(1) beyond it

code: Arrays.sort(iv, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));   // the sorted list, with [4,8] dropped in
if (out.isEmpty() || cur[0] > out.get(out.size() - 1)[1]) out.add(new int[]{ cur[0], cur[1] });
// otherwise it overlaps the block being built, so stretch that block's end

commonMistakes: Using `intervals[i][1] <= start` in phase 1. With inclusive ends, an interval ending exactly at the new start touches it and must be absorbed, not copied; the strict `<` is what sends it into phase 2.
Comparing against the original `newInterval[1]` in phase 2 instead of the running `end`. The new interval grows as it absorbs, and the next interval must be tested against the widened block.
Appending the merged interval inside the phase-2 loop, which emits it once per absorbed interval. It is appended exactly once, after the loop.
Forgetting the empty-input and no-overlap cases: with `intervals = []` the answer is just the new interval, and a new interval that overlaps nothing still has to be inserted in the right place.
Mutating the input arrays when widening — `intervals[i][1] = end` writes through to the caller's data. Build a fresh `int[]` for the merged block.

Assuming a binary search for the insertion point changes the complexity. It finds the start faster, but phase 2 may still absorb O(n) intervals and the copy is O(n) regardless; it is a constant-factor win, not an asymptotic one.
